mechaber/1:main: The law of chametz found in a Jew's shop where the workers are non-Jews, or vice versa. Contains 1 seif. A Jew's shop and its inventory (meaning the merchandise and shop utensils) belonging to a Jew, and the workers who enter there are non-Jews — chametz found there after Pesach is forbidden in benefit. A non-Jew's shop and inventory of a non-Jew, and workers who enter there are Jews — chametz found there is permitted even for eating. This is the text of Rashi and Rabbenu Hai; but Rabbenu Chananel reads the opposite.
baer-heitev/1:א: Forbidden in benefit. And if chametz is found on the road immediately after Pesach and we do not know whether it belongs to a non-Jew or a Jew — it is forbidden in eating and permitted in benefit (Beit Chadash and Magen Avraham — see there; and see siman 446 seif 4). Kaf HaChayim disagrees and raised: if the majority are Jews it is forbidden, and if half-and-half, and all the more so if the majority are non-Jews, it is permitted even in eating for one who is not careful about pat akum; and likewise any doubt regarding chametz that passed over Pesach is permitted even in eating — see there.
baer-heitev/1:ב: The opposite. Taz wrote that in every case we follow the lenient view, for there is no penalty here.
chok-yaakov/1:_: A Jew's shop. The Rif, Rambam, Rosh, and other poskim omitted these laws entirely. Raavad in Temim De'im siman 245 in his hasagot on Baal HaMaor wrote that he omitted this law because there are variant texts and we rule stringently — end quote. In truth it appears to say the opposite from the fact that these poskim omitted it and did not teach us a prohibition, for they hold one may be lenient from a doubt like any d'rabbanan doubt; therefore they were not concerned to write it since it is permitted. Unlike if there were a hint of prohibition — then they would have to mention and warn about the prohibition. Bach implies that even in a doubt where Pesach passed one should forbid eating and permit benefit, and likewise Magen Avraham, and that this is the implication of Tosafot and Rashi in Eruvin daf 64 — see there. In my humble opinion, as I wrote, from the words of Tosafot and Rashi there is no proof at all; on the contrary it appears from their words to the contrary. Magen Avraham seems to have understood Tosafot's intent as Ateret Zekenim explained in siman 31 to settle their words — but in truth his words are very forced in Tosafot's intent here; Maharsha there also did not fulfill the obligation of explaining Tosafot's words. In my humble opinion Tosafot's intent is clear and simple: to settle the sugya in the Gemara regarding chametz found after Pesach that they permitted in benefit and forbade in eating — from which we learn we follow the majority of passersby who are non-Jews; for otherwise, if it were only a doubt whether it belongs to a Jew or non-Jew, eating should also be permitted, and one cannot say that since he has permission only because we may suspect it belongs to a non-Jew, therefore eating is properly forbidden since it is bread of a non-Jew as Tosafot wrote there — in any event we do not follow passersby for this. Tosafot wrote: nevertheless eating should be permitted since we may suspect it belongs to a Jew and occurred after Pesach; rather we certainly follow the majority of passersby. It is proven explicitly from Tosafot's intent that in doubt of chametz that passed Pesach one may permit even in eating. There is no contradiction from what Tosafot wrote in the following discussion "and we learned" etc. that if chametz of a non-Jew after Pesach is forbidden in benefit it should be forbidden from doubt lest it became so during Pesach — end quote. This is no contradiction to what was said first, for Tosafot's intent is thus: if you say chametz of a non-Jew after Pesach is forbidden, then the penalty reason does not apply to them at all, and perforce you must say they hold like R' Yehudah that even after Pesach one violates a Torah prohibition of chametz that passed Pesach, as in the chapter Kol Sha'ah, and not like R' Acha bar Yaakov; if so it would be a Torah doubt and stringently — but in truth we hold chametz that passed Pesach is d'rabbanan, so we follow leniency in doubt, and so appears Maharsha's view there in Chadashei Tosafot that one may be lenient in doubt even in eating, though he is very forced there in explaining Tosafot. Also Ateret Zekenim deviated from our acceptance. The principle in our hands is d'rabbanan doubt is lenient; all fits. So appears somewhat in the sugya in Chullin daf 4 per what the Gemara there thought regarding chametz of sinners that one may be lenient in this doubt like any d'rabbanan doubt — see Tosafot there. We have merited the law from this sugya: chametz found on the road immediately after Pesach — if the majority of passersby are Jews it is forbidden; if half-and-half, and all the more so if the majority are non-Jews, it is permitted even in eating for one not careful about pat akum; and likewise any doubt of chametz that passed Pesach — this is the main ruling.
dagul-merevavah/1:_: His intent is from Rashi's and Tosafot's explanation — proof that we follow the majority of passersby, from that they forbade in eating; therefore Tosafot there had to explain at the end of "that we follow" that if it belonged to a Jew one could attribute it to after Pesach — but it is better to explain that it deals immediately after Pesach and it cannot be attributed to having occurred after Pesach, and then automatically it is proven we follow the majority of passersby from that they permitted in benefit. But certainly regarding benefit, even if we do not follow the majority of passersby, nevertheless it is permitted in benefit — see Maharsha there.
eliyah-rabbah/1:_: (1) chametz found, etc. Magen Avraham wrote: chametz found after Pesach — if the majority of the city are Samaritans it is permitted; and likewise on the road if the majority of passersby are Samaritans; and even if the majority are Jews, if it is in a matter where one can attribute it to having occurred after Pesach, it is permitted. And regarding doubt of chametz that passed Pesach — Bach and Magen Avraham hold it is forbidden in eating and permitted in benefit; Chok Yaakov holds it is permitted in eating, for d'rabbanan doubt is lenient. He explained what Tosafot wrote in Eruvin daf 64 s.v. velamadnu etc. that it should be forbidden from doubt — meaning according to what occurred to him that chametz of Samaritans after Pesach is forbidden in benefit, perforce it is d'oraisa like R' Yehudah in chapter Kol Sha'ah, for Samaritan cooking has no d'rabbanan penalty, and he is correct. Maharsha and Ateret Zekenim wondered for nothing — see there. But what he explained in s.v. sheholkhin etc. — see there — is forced. Also what Maharsha and other commentators troubled themselves to wonder — it seems to me it is no difficulty, for one can say Tosafot holds like Baal HaItur that I brought above: chametz of a Jew that passed Pesach that he nullified is permitted in benefit, and presumably he nullified; and even though it deals when he nullified, nevertheless we say presumably he nullified; and furthermore it should only be a doubt like a doubt-of-a-doubt — requires study. One can also say perhaps Tosafot can prove from that they did not forbid in benefit — perhaps they hold Rabban Gamliel like R' Shimon according to R' Acha in Pesachim daf 29 and permit even d'rabbanan chametz of a Jew that passed Pesach if not that we must say they permit even in eating; and in truth perhaps Rabban Gamliel holds they penalized d'rabbanan only in eating, as Rava holds they penalized even in benefit; if so one cannot prove from that they did not forbid in benefit — requires study.
kaf-hachayyim/1:_: (1) [Seif 1] A Jew's shop and inventory of a Jew, etc. This is the text of Rashi and R' Hai, but Rabbenu Chananel reads the opposite. The rule: for Rashi and R' Hai we follow the shop owner — if the shop owner is a Jew, chametz found there after Pesach is forbidden in benefit; if the shop owner is a non-Jew, it is permitted. For Rabbenu Chananel we follow the workers — if the workers who enter there are Jews, chametz found there after Pesach is forbidden in benefit; if they are non-Jews, it is permitted in benefit, as explained explicitly in the words of Rashi and Rabbenu Chananel — see there.
machatzit-hashekel/1:_: (s.k. 1) And inventory — meaning merchandise. Meaning to exclude that it requires specifically that the inventory be bread; rather in all merchandise the law is so.
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (1) The meaning of the merchandise — and it deals when the merchandise was bread and wine and the like.
mishnah-berurah/1:ג: (3) Forbidden in benefit — for we attribute that this chametz belongs to the shop and not to the workers, even though they are accustomed to be there, because the chametz in the shop is fixed there regularly, and it is more plausible to attribute that it remained there from his chametz that he did not find at the time of bedikah; and plainly it deals when he found it immediately after Pesach in a matter where one cannot attribute that the chametz is from now.
mishnah-berurah/1:ד: (4) Permitted even in eating — meaning even if the shop was closed all the days of Pesach, so there is nothing to attribute that the non-Jewish owner of the shop brought this chametz there on Pesach, and certainly this chametz is from before Pesach. And one might think there is concern to attribute the chametz found there that it is from the Jewish workers who are always there, that they forgot it there before Pesach — it teaches us we do not say so.
mishnah-berurah/1:ה: (5) Reads the opposite — for he holds we attribute more to the workers who are always there, whether for leniency or stringency; and for the law we hold like the first view. And some wrote they do not disagree at all, and the second view speaks only when there were no foodstuffs in the shop but only other merchandise; but if there were foodstuffs in the shop, even according to this view we follow the shop for chametz found there, as it is fixed regularly. chametz found after Pesach and we do not know if it belongs to a non-Jew or a Jew — there are opinions among later authorities: some wrote it is permitted in benefit and forbidden in eating; and some are lenient and say it is permitted even in eating, as any d'rabbanan doubt where we follow leniency. And if in that place most Jews are present, it is forbidden in benefit, for it certainly fell from a Jew; and all this when found immediately after Pesach, or the bread is old so one cannot say it was baked after Pesach. But if one can attribute that it fell after Pesach, it is permitted even in eating in every case, for it is more plausible to attribute that it is after Pesach than to say it fell from a Jew before Pesach, for such a long time it would not have lain on the road.
peri-megadim/1:ב: If one gives his animal after Pesach to a mumar who knows he will certainly feed it chametz that passed Pesach — forbidden; and in doubt during Pesach also permitted, as siman 448 in Magen Avraham 10 and Pri Chadash there regarding one who throws benefit-value to the Dead Sea; and in Yoreh De'ah siman 1 it does not imply so — see there he wrote b'dieved permitted.
magen-avraham/1:ב: Forbidden in benefit. For we attribute it to the shop owner; and for Rabbenu Chananel we attribute to the workers. It appears from Bach's words that chametz found after Pesach and we do not know if it belongs to a non-Jew or Jew — forbidden in eating and permitted in benefit — see there; and so in Eruvin daf 64b in Rashi and Tosafot: if we did not follow the majority of passersby and we would attribute to a Jew, nevertheless it would be permitted in benefit; and it is proven from there that we follow the majority, meaning the majority of the city as explained in Yoreh De'ah siman 1; and if it is in a matter where one can attribute that it occurred after Pesach, even where the majority are Jews it is permitted (Tosafot there; and see chapter 1 of Chullin).
peri-megadim/1:א: So — Taz Pesachim 41b, and Beit Yosef explains Rabbenu Chananel reads the opposite and we follow the workers and judge as certain. Jewish workers — to forbid in benefit; non-Jewish workers — to permit in eating; it also deals when the inventory is bread and wine, nevertheless we follow the workers entirely; and for Rashi we follow the inventory of whom it belongs entirely — see there. Taz challenged Rabbenu Chananel: granted with non-Jewish workers it is permitted in eating from doubt and it is not a fixed shop for this purpose — still, non-Jewish inventory and Jewish workers, why forbidden and it is not a doubt to permit? This is what Taz wrote: why do we attribute more to workers than the shop, and let it be a doubt to permit in eating? As appears from the beginning of his words that Rashi is satisfied with non-Jewish inventory that it is a doubt and nevertheless permitted in eating — unlike Magen Avraham letter 2, and it will be explained there. And on this Taz wrote that Rabbenu Chananel agrees with Rashi regarding bread inventory — we attribute to whom the inventory belongs; and Rabbenu Chananel deals with inventory of other merchandise; if so according to Rashi and Rabbenu Chananel and Tur and Mechaber it appears they disagree, and he concludes they disagree regarding bread inventory: for Rabbenu Chananel it is a doubt and permitted in eating, for doubt of chametz that passed Pesach is d'rabbanan (where they eat pat akum); for Rashi the inventory is primary and Jewish inventory is certainly forbidden. It follows that regarding inventory of other merchandise, all follow the workers, for the majority is not following the shop owner even though he eats there sometimes. For bread inventory according to Rashi we follow the inventory, and if it belongs to a Jew it is certainly forbidden; for Rabbenu Chananel it is a doubt and permitted. It follows that for the law, in all cases it appears permitted, for it is a legal doubt; except it is like a double doubt — perhaps the halacha is like Rashi and it is certain. If you say like Rabbenu Chananel it is still a doubt perhaps it belongs to a Jew; and in Yoreh De'ah 110 we wrote in s.v. stringently for d'rabbanan (and see Pri Chadash in Klalim s.v. in one matter these stringencies combine — requires study in two rabbinic disputes). Levush explains like Beit Yosef and Bach — see Ateret Zekenim. Baer Heitev letter 2 wrote: Taz wrote in every case leniently — see there; this is for Rabbenu Chananel, but for the law one can say it is like a double doubt as written. Ohr HaChayim wrote Rabbenu Chananel's reason regarding bread inventory that we attribute to workers for they are the majority like coins before cattle merchants — see there; one can say there we follow the majority of buyers not sellers, unlike here where the majority of chametz is the inventory. See Temim De'im siman 245 daf 74b: Maharshal omitted the Rif's baraita of the shop because there are variant texts and all forbid; it implies there even in benefit; and furthermore otherwise it should still bring benefit, and it is difficult: if so, doubt should be forbidden in eating as Magen Avraham wrote regarding benefit, why forbidden — for the halacha is like R' Shimon and d'rabbanan doubt is lenient.
peri-megadim/1:ג: See Pri Megadim siman 10 regarding one who gives his ox to a non-Jew and the non-Jew accepted responsibility — forbidden, for nevertheless it stands in a Jew's domain, unlike the Mechaber in siman 446 seif 4; nevertheless on Pesach it is permitted, for the non-Jew intends for his own benefit if he shares the offspring with him — see there. And likewise one who rents a horse to a non-Jew on the intermediate days of Pesach and knows the non-Jew will give chametz as wine — as explained above, the non-Jew's benefit is suspended, he does not have benefit from this — see there; requires study for the law. And what he wrote there that since the Mechaber wrote the view of those who permit first, it seems his view is so — I wrote in Klalim in Yoreh De'ah this is when writing one view anonymously; but some say letter Aleph and letter Aleph regarding Torah stringently and in the matter of doubt leniently — see Magen Avraham 446 seif 16 and it will be explained further in Notes.
turei-zahav/1:_: This is Rashi's text. In shop and inventory we attribute; and this inventory means bread and wine sold in the shop; therefore it works in a non-Jew's shop, for in any case the workers also bring bread there, and it is a doubt; one can say since we hold like R' Shimon that chametz after Pesach is forbidden d'rabbanan as a penalty, here the penalty does not apply except in a Jew's shop, for we go stringently and need a reason why; and it appears the shop's chametz is certainly fixed and placed there, while the workers' is occasional — one can say what they bring there they eat entirely; therefore we follow the shop. Rabbenu Chananel reads the opposite and follows the workers; it is certainly difficult why we attribute more to workers than the shop, since in the shop the chametz is more fixed; and if for Rabbenu Chananel it deals when there is no bread in the shop only other merchandise, then there is no difference between Rashi and Rabbenu Chananel; it is possible this difference exists between them: for Rabbenu Chananel it deals when there is only merchandise not bread, and if there were bread in the shop we would say it is a doubt; and in every case we follow leniency, for there is no penalty here.
